newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-National Jet keen on Indonesia link.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-National Jet keen on Indonesia link.

text.p: Australia's third largest airline operator National Jet Systems (NJS) sees a new contract with Merpati Nusantara Airlines, a subsidiary of Indonesia's national carrier Garuda, as a key stepping stone into Asia.

NJS founder, managing director and co-owner Warren Seymour told Reuters that under the 10-year contract, which began this month, his company would provide up to 15 British Aerospace 146 aircraft plus pilots, engineer training, and maintenance.
"They (Merpati) operate them, task them and are responsible for putting people in them," Seymour said in a recent interview.
He said that the deal - which he declined to quantify - was fundamental to the company's future involvement in the region.
"I have got a vision that our future lies in that area (through these sorts of contracts)," he said.

Seymour also said the company was in negotiation with the Indonesian state-owned aircraft company, Industri Pesawat Terbang Nusantara (IPTN), to train personnel to establish coastal surveillance operations in other southeast Asian countries.

A former pilot in the Australian outback city of Alice Springs, Seymour founded NJS in Adelaide in 1990, buying and leasing jets on the back of contracts which began with ferrying Santos Ltd workers to the Moomba gas fields in South Australia.
His partner is Adele Lloyd, who took over the role from her late husband Guy, the founder of Lloyd Aviation.

While Seymour has described NJS as a family organisation with a very flat management structure - until recently he personally interviewed all pilots and flight attendants - its rapid rise as a niche service provider and potential growth are likely soon to see a new approach.

Seymour said NJS was now introducing corporate governance procedures, a new management structure, and was set to appoint two external directors ahead of possibly inviting institutional investors to take an equity position.
"I think our expansion into southeast Asia is going to require some hard cash...just in start-up costs, bringing in the right people, carrying them till they start generating cash.
"I am hoping within the next year, hopefully by the end of this financial year, we will be in a position to invite people to have a look," he said.

However Seymour insisted, as always, that any expansion in Australia or offshore will continue to follow the company's policy of seeking strategic support roles, and that it had it no intention of a head-to-head challenge to major airlines.
NJS has 22 bases through Australia, Papua New Guinea and Indonesia, employing nearly 800 people, and a fleet of 45 aircraft, including 17 BAe146s and one Avro RJ70 jet.
The company would have revenue in 1996/97 of around A$180 million, Seymour said.

The company has the Australian government's Coastwatch contract, reported to be worth A$300 million over ten years, but recently lost a A$6 million training support programme with the Defence Department.

NJS is a major player in independent and contract niche air services, running the Airlink service for Qantas Airways Ltd across Australia and operating the Australia Post/Qantas joint venture Australian Air Express, as well as its own regional services in northern and western Australia.
It also fuels the resource sector, with fly in-fly out operations in Australia for MIM Ltd, Santos Ltd, CRA Ltd, Newcrest Ltd, and to BHP Ltd's Ok Tedi mine in Papua New Guinea.
This year NJS opened a service to the remote Indian Ocean territory of Christmas Island and Singapore and the Indonesian resort island of Bali, via the East Java city of Surabaya.
In October the service flew return to Darwin via Lombok, which had a strong tourist attraction and was the proposed site for a major mining operation by Newmont Mining Ltd, he said.

Seymour said the Christmas Island run, which carries many gambling enthusiasts to the island's popular casino, had been a major boost for the company, giving it credibility in the region, and bringing it close to operators like Merpati.

Back home, Seymour said the company was trying to develop Adelaide into a base of expertise in heavy aircraft maintenance for BAe 146s, a move already approved by the Indonesian government which would allow Merpati craft to be serviced there.
NJS is also considered by industry sources to be in a prime position for any outsourcing proposed by Qantas and Ansett Australia, as the major carriers seek to reduce costs.
